Sandisk’s 256GB card, meanwhile, is available for $49.99 ($10 off Amazon’s typical list price) from Amazon and Sandisk , if you prefer one brand over the other for some reason. articles.title: A Refund Changed the Customer’s Eligibility. How Does the API Know?
articles.excerpt: A customer has Gold membership and three completed purchases. That's enough to qualify for a rewards offer. Then one of those purchases is refunded. The business decision has changed. But what happens…
articles.body: A customer has Gold membership and three completed purchases. That's enough to qualify for a rewards offer. Then one of those purchases is refunded. The business decision has changed. But what happens to the data that powers the Rewards API—and the AI agent relying on that API? This is a useful example of a broader data architecture challenge: How do we keep operational read models current as source data changes? The architectural pattern Consider a simple flow: PostgreSQL → Change Data Capture → Incremental SQL → Maintained Eligibility View → Rewards API → AI Agent Here's what happens: 1. The source changes. A refund is recorded in PostgreSQL, changing the business state that determines customer eligibility. 2. CDC captures the change.

articles.title: Compressing a PDF to an exact file size (like 200 KB) in the browser with WebAssembly
articles.excerpt: Every government portal, job site and university application seems to have the same rule: "Upload a PDF, max 200 KB." Then you scan a two-page form on your phone and get a 4 MB file. I built KaiPDF, a…
articles.body: Every government portal, job site and university application seems to have the same rule: "Upload a PDF, max 200 KB." Then you scan a two-page form on your phone and get a 4 MB file. I built KaiPDF, a free in-browser PDF toolkit; this is how one part of it works: the "make it smaller than X" mode of the compressor. Everything below runs in the browser tab. The file is never uploaded. Why upload portals have size limits The limits are rarely about the PDF itself. They come from older systems behind the form: Database blobs and mail gateways. Many back offices store attachments in a database column or forward them by email, where 200 KB to 2 MB was a safe number years ago. Bandwidth for reviewers. A clerk opening 500 applications a day doesn't want 5 MB each. Defence against junk.

articles.title: The MCP context tax: I measured what tool definitions cost your context window (21,328 MCP servers)
articles.excerpt: Originally published on Serverdex, where the numbers update live. Here's a cost most people never see: every MCP tool definition is loaded into your model's context before it does any work. Connect a…
articles.body: Originally published on Serverdex , where the numbers update live. Here's a cost most people never see: every MCP tool definition is loaded into your model's context before it does any work. Connect a server, and its tools' names, descriptions and full argument schemas are sent to the model on every single turn — before it reads your prompt. Ten lean tools are cheap. One server with two hundred verbose tools is a standing bill you pay on every message. Nobody had measured that bill across the ecosystem, so I did. I called tools/list on every public MCP server that answers — no API key, no OAuth — and measured the tool and token footprint.

articles.title: AI Rate Limiting for LLM Calls in TypeScript
articles.excerpt: You fire 50 LLM calls at once. A batch job, a fan out over documents, a busy hour. The provider only lets 10 through at a time, so the rest come back as 429 Too Many Requests. The usual fix is to retr…
articles.body: You fire 50 LLM calls at once. A batch job, a fan out over documents, a busy hour. The provider only lets 10 through at a time, so the rest come back as 429 Too Many Requests . The usual fix is to retry 429s with backoff. That helps, but notice what it means: every retry is a request you sent after you already got rate limited. You are reacting to a limit you could have stayed under. This post shows the difference with real numbers and how to rate limit LLM calls in TypeScript with VernLLM , before the provider says no. Retrying 429s vs not causing them I ran a 50 call burst against a scripted provider that accepts 10 requests in flight and rejects the rest with 429. Both runs used maxRetries: 2 .

articles.body: A few months ago, I wrote an article titled “I Reduced Prisma Database Operations by 60% Without Upgrading My Database” . In that post, I shared how profiling slow queries with EXPLAIN ANALYZE helped us cut database operations on my project, Sellary ( sellary.in )—a digital commerce platform for Indian creators. Shortly after publishing it, Martin Janse van Rensburg from the Prisma team reached out with an intriguing challenge: "Since you already use Prisma ORM, would you be up for a follow-up running Sellary on the whole Prisma platform, adding Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute , with an AI agent doing the setup?" Martin offered two months of trial credits and asked for an honest, unfiltered take: setup experience, developer experience, latency, pricing, and what broke along the way.

articles.title: The 2026 Developer's Guide to Agent Fleets: Taming Unbounded Concurrency with Bounded Worker Pools
articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. Agent fleets fail in a peculiar way: they work beautifully in a demo, then collapse under production traffic. The code looks reasonable. You spawn a task for every i…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . Agent fleets fail in a peculiar way: they work beautifully in a demo, then collapse under production traffic. The code looks reasonable. You spawn a task for every incoming request, every document chunk, every sub-agent. Each task calls a model, retries on failure, waits on a tool, and spawns more work. Throughput rises until something saturates: connection pools, rate limits, memory, your monthly budget, or the provider's willingness to serve you. The fix is not to make agents faster. It is to make concurrency a bounded resource , not an emergent side effect of application logic.

articles.title: Stop Giving AI Agents Your Admin Credentials
articles.excerpt: The Problem Is Not the Agent. It's the Key You Gave It. In 2026, AI coding pipelines are no longer experimental. Teams are running them against real repositories, real deployment targets, and real clo…
articles.body: The Problem Is Not the Agent. It's the Key You Gave It. In 2026, AI coding pipelines are no longer experimental. Teams are running them against real repositories, real deployment targets, and real cloud accounts. The security question that keeps surfacing is not whether these systems work. It's what happens when a pipeline that can push to production also has read access to your .env files, your shell history, and your AWS root key. According to Gartner's The State of AI in DevOps: Security and Governance Challenges ( source ), organizations deploying AI systems in DevOps environments face significant security risks from credential exposure, and maintaining compliance requires zero-trust authentication patterns combined with dedicated secrets management.

articles.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
articles.excerpt: A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.
articles.body: The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A t otal solar eclipse will sweep across the country , passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date . We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps. Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it.

articles.body: Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space. The new report focuses on China , Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon . The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain . articles.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.
articles.body: A snapshot of the Himalayas captured from aboard the ISS. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.
